A note on idempotents in quandle rings

Dilpreet Kaur Email address: dilpreetkaur@iitj.ac.in Address: Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur N.H. 62, Nagaur Road, Karwar Jodhpur 342030 Rajasthan and Pushpendra Singh Email address: pushpendra@iisermohali.ac.in Address: Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Mohali, Sector 81, Mohali 140306, India
Date: August 29, 2026
Abstract.

It was conjectured that the nonzero idempotents of the integral quandle ring of a finite latin quandle are trivial. We prove this holds for latin dihedral quandles. Furthermore, we discuss counterexamples against this conjecture.

Key words and phrases: 
Quandles, Quandle rings, Affine quandles
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
17D99,20N02

1. Introduction

A quandle is an algebraic structure (Q,⊳)(Q,\triangleright) where the binary operation satisfies the following properties.

  1. (1)

    The map Rx:Q→Q,Rx​(y)=y⊳xR_{x}:Q\rightarrow Q,~R_{x}(y)=y\triangleright x is an automorphism for all x∈Qx\in Q.

  2. (2)

    Rx​(x)=xR_{x}(x)=x for all x∈Qx\in Q.

An affine quandle Aff⁡(A,f){\rm Aff}(A,f) is an additive abelian group AA with f∈Aut⁡(A)f\in{\rm Aut}(A) with quandle operation x⊳y=f⁡(x)+(1−f)​(y)x\triangleright y=f(x)+(1-f)(y). In particular, if A=ℤnA=\mathbb{Z}_{n} and f⁡(x)=−xf(x)=-x, then the affine quandle is known as a dihedral quandle. We denote it by ℛn\mathcal{R}_{n}.

A quandle ring is defined analogously to a group ring. It is introduced in [1]. Let KK be an associative ring. Consider the following set of finite linear combinations.

K⁡[Q]={∑iax​x;ax∈K,x∈Q}K[Q]=\left\{\sum\limits_{i}a_{x}x\;;a_{x}\in K,x\in Q\right\}

Then K⁡[Q]K[Q] forms an abelian group with the usual addition. The following multiplication equips it with a ring structure.

(∑xax​x)⋅(∑yby​y)=∑x,yax​by​(x⊳y)\left(\sum\limits_{x}a_{x}x\right)\cdot\left(\sum\limits_{y}b_{y}y\right)=\sum\limits_{x,y}a_{x}b_{y}(x\triangleright y)

The mapping ε:K⁡[Q]→K,∑xax​x↦∑xax\varepsilon:K[Q]\rightarrow K,\sum\limits_{x}a_{x}x\mapsto\sum\limits_{x}a_{x} is a ring homomorphism. This is known as augmentation mapping.

The authors give various results about quandles QQ by studying properties of K⁡[Q]K[Q]. Furthermore, the authors in [3] and [2] study the idempotent elements of K⁡[Q]K[Q] and give applications of idempotents in knot theory for the construction of invariants of knots and links. In particular, they state the following conjectures.

Conjecture 1.1.

[2, Conjecture 3.10] The integral quandle ring of a semi-latin quandle has only trivial idempotents. In particular, the integral quandle ring of a finite latin quandle has only trivial idempotents.

Conjecture 1.2.

[3, Conjecture 7.6] The Peirce spectrum of the complex quandle algebra of the dihedral quandle of odd order is {0,1,−1}\{0,1,-1\}.

In the section 2, we prove that the integral quandle ring of latin dihedral quandles has only trivial idempotents. Furthermore, in section 3, we compute the Peirce spectrum of ℂ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}] for nn odd. In section 4, we show that for an integral ring of affine connected quandles of prime order, we can construct infinitely many nontrivial idempotents given a nontrivial idempotent.

2. Idempotents in ℤ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{Z}[\mathcal{R}_{n}]

The dihedral quandle ℛn\mathcal{R}_{n} is a latin quandle for nn odd. In this section, we assume that nn is odd. The quandle operation on ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} is x⊳y=2​y−xx\triangleright y=2y-x.

The quandle ring ℤ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{Z}[\mathcal{R}_{n}] is a free ℤ\mathbb{Z}-module with basis {ex;x∈ℛn}\{e_{x}\;;x\in\mathcal{R}_{n}\} with the multiplication on basis elements given as ex​ey=ex⊳y=e2​y−xe_{x}e_{y}=e_{x\triangleright y}=e_{2y-x}. The mapping x↦exx\mapsto e_{x} is an embedding of quandle ℛn\mathcal{R}_{n} into ℤ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{Z}[\mathcal{R}_{n}].

Let u=∑x∈ℤnax​exu=\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{x}e_{x} be an element in ℤ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{Z}[\mathcal{R}_{n}]. We solve u2=uu^{2}=u and find the coefficients axa_{x}.

u2=(∑x∈ℤnax​ex)⋅(∑y∈ℤnay​ey)\displaystyle u^{2}=\left(\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{x}e_{x}\right)\cdot\left(\sum\limits_{y\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{y}e_{y}\right) =∑x,y∈ℤnax​ay​e2​y−x\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{x,y\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{x}a_{y}e_{2y-x}
=∑y,z∈ℤna2​y−z​ay​ez\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{y,z\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{2y-z}a_{y}e_{z}

Let u2=∑z∈ℤncz​ezu^{2}=\sum\limits_{z\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}c_{z}e_{z}, then we have cz=∑y∈ℤna2​y−z​ayc_{z}=\sum\limits_{y\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{2y-z}a_{y}. The equality u2=uu^{2}=u means

az=∑y∈ℤna2​y−z​ay for all ​z∈ℤna_{z}=\sum\limits_{y\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{2y-z}a_{y}\quad\quad\text{ for all }z\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}

We solve the above system of equations using fourier transform on ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}. Let ζ=ei​2​π/n\zeta=e^{i2\pi/n}. Using the coefficients of uu, define a map a^:ℤn→ℂ,r↦∑x∈ℤnax​ζr​x\hat{a}:\mathbb{Z}_{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{C},r\mapsto\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{x}\zeta^{rx}.

Lemma 2.1.

Let x,y∈ℛnx,y\in\mathcal{R}_{n}. Then

∑r∈ℤnζr⁡(x−y)={n​ if ​x=y0​ if ​x≠y\sum\limits_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\zeta^{r(x-y)}=\begin{cases}n\text{ if }x=y\\ 0\text{ if }x\neq y\end{cases}
Proof.

The expression gives nn for x=yx=y. For x≠yx\neq y, let q=ζx−yq=\zeta^{x-y}. Then q≠1q\neq 1. We have ∑r∈ℤnqr=qn−1q−1=0\sum\limits_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}q^{r}=\frac{q^{n}-1}{q-1}=0, since qn=1q^{n}=1. ∎

Lemma 2.2.

Let x∈ℛnx\in\mathcal{R}_{n}. Then we have

ax=1n​∑r∈ℤna^​(r)​ζ−r​xa_{x}=\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\hat{a}(r)\zeta^{-rx}

Furthermore,

∑r∈ℤn|a^​(r)|2=n​∑x∈ℤnax2\sum\limits_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}|\hat{a}(r)|^{2}=n\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{x}^{2}
Proof.

Expanding rhs by substituting for a^​(r)\hat{a}(r), we get

1n​∑r∈ℤna^​(r)​ζ−r​x=1n​∑r,y∈ℤnay​ζr​y​ζ−r​x=1n​∑y∈ℤnay​∑r∈ℤnζr⁡(y−x)=ax\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\hat{a}(r)\zeta^{-rx}=\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{r,y\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{y}\zeta^{ry}\zeta^{-rx}=\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{y\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{y}\sum\limits_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\zeta^{r(y-x)}=a_{x}

where the last equality follows using Lemma 2.1. Now we have

∑r∈ℤn|a^​(r)|2=∑r∈ℤna^​(r)​a^​(r)¯\displaystyle\sum\limits_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}|\hat{a}(r)|^{2}=\sum\limits_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\hat{a}(r)\overline{\hat{a}(r)} =∑r∈ℤn(∑x∈ℤnax​ζr​x)​(∑y∈ℤnay¯​ζ−r​y)\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\left(\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{x}\zeta^{rx}\right)\left(\sum\limits_{y\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\bar{a_{y}}\zeta^{-ry}\right)
=∑x,y∈ℤnax​ay​∑r∈ℤnζr⁡(x−y)=n​∑x∈ℤnax2\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{x,y\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{x}a_{y}\sum\limits_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\zeta^{r(x-y)}=n\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{x}^{2}

∎

Now using coefficients of u2u^{2}, we define function c^:ℤn→ℂ,r↦∑z∈ℤncz​ζr​z\hat{c}:\mathbb{Z}_{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{C},r\mapsto\sum\limits_{z\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}c_{z}\zeta^{rz}.

Lemma 2.3.

Let u2=uu^{2}=u. Then a^​(r)=a^​(−r)​a^​(2​r)\hat{a}(r)=\hat{a}(-r)\hat{a}(2r).

Proof.

Substituting for czc_{z} in c^​(r)\hat{c}(r), we get

c^​(r)=∑z∈ℤn(∑y∈ℤna2​y−z​ay)​ζr​z\hat{c}(r)=\sum\limits_{z\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\left(\sum\limits_{y\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{2y-z}a_{y}\right)\zeta^{rz}

Put x=2​y−zx=2y-z, then we have

c^​(r)\displaystyle\hat{c}(r) =∑x,y∈ℤnax​ay​ζr⁡(2​y−x)\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{x,y\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{x}a_{y}\zeta^{r(2y-x)}
=(∑x∈ℤnax​ζ−r​x)⋅(∑y∈ℤnay​ζ2​r​y)\displaystyle=\left(\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{x}\zeta^{-rx}\right)\cdot\left(\sum\limits_{y\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{y}\zeta^{2ry}\right)
=a^​(−r)​a^​(2​r)\displaystyle=\hat{a}(-r)\hat{a}(2r)

Now u2=uu^{2}=u implies cz=azc_{z}=a_{z} for all z∈ℤnz\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}, and so c^​(r)=a^​(r)\hat{c}(r)=\hat{a}(r). Thus a^​(r)=a^​(−r)​a^​(2​r)\hat{a}(r)=\hat{a}(-r)\hat{a}(2r) for all r∈ℤnr\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}. ∎

Now, below we work under the condition that u2=uu^{2}=u.

Lemma 2.4.

Let nn be odd, then for r∈ℤnr\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}, either a^​(r)=0\hat{a}(r)=0 or |a^​(r)|=1|\hat{a}(r)|=1.

Proof.

We have a^​(−r)=a^​(r)¯\hat{a}(-r)=\overline{\hat{a}(r)}. Let a^​(r)¯≠0\overline{\hat{a}(r)}\neq 0. Then, by the previous lemma, we have a^​(2​r)=a^​(r)a^​(r)¯\hat{a}(2r)=\frac{\hat{a}(r)}{\overline{\hat{a}(r)}} and so |a^​(2​r)|=1|\hat{a}(2r)|=1. Repeating this, we get |a^​(2j​r)|=1|\hat{a}(2^{j}r)|=1 for all j≥1j\geq 1. Since nn is odd, so for some jj value, 2j​r≡r(modn)2^{j}r\equiv r\pmod{n} and so |a^​(r)|=1|\hat{a}(r)|=1. Thus either a^​(r)=0\hat{a}(r)=0 or |a^​(r)|=1|\hat{a}(r)|=1. ∎

Theorem 2.5.

The set of idempotents of ℤ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{Z}[\mathcal{R}_{n}] for nn odd is {0,ex;x∈ℛn}\{0,e_{x}\;;x\in\mathcal{R}_{n}\}.

Proof.

Continuing with previous notations, let mm be the size of set {r∈ℤn;a^​(r)≠0}\{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}\;;\hat{a}(r)\neq 0\}. Then using Lemma 2.2 and Lemma 2.4, we get

m=n​∑x∈ℤnax2m=n\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{x}^{2}

Since 0≤m≤n0\leq m\leq n and ∑xax2\sum\limits_{x}a_{x}^{2} is a non-negative integer, so m=0m=0 or m=nm=n. Since uu is an idempotent, under the augmentation map we have ε⁡(u)=0\varepsilon(u)=0 or ε⁡(u)=1\varepsilon(u)=1.

If ε⁡(u)=0\varepsilon(u)=0, then a^​(0)=∑xax=0\hat{a}(0)=\sum\limits_{x}a_{x}=0 Then m=|{a^​(r)≠0;r∈ℤn}|≤n−1m=|\{\hat{a}(r)\neq 0\;;r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}\}|\leq n-1. So m=0m=0. This implies a^​(r)=0\hat{a}(r)=0 for all r∈ℤnr\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}. By using Lemma 2.2, we get ax=0a_{x}=0 for all x∈ℛnx\in\mathcal{R}_{n} and so u=0u=0.

If ε⁡(u)=1\varepsilon(u)=1, then a^​(0)=∑xax=1\hat{a}(0)=\sum\limits_{x}a_{x}=1. Then m=|{a^​(r)≠0;r∈ℤn}|≥1m=|\{\hat{a}(r)\neq 0\;;r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}\}|\geq 1. So m=nm=n. This implies ∑xax2=1\sum\limits_{x}a_{x}^{2}=1. Since axa_{x} for all x∈ℛnx\in\mathcal{R}_{n} are integers, so the only solutions are ax=1a_{x}=1 for x∈ℛnx\in\mathcal{R}_{n} and ay=0a_{y}=0 for all x≠y∈ℛnx\neq y\in\mathcal{R}_{n}. Thus u=ex,x∈ℛnu=e_{x},\;x\in\mathcal{R}_{n}.

∎

3. Peirce Spectrum of ℂ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}]

Let ℂ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}] be the complex quandle algebra of the dihedral quandle of odd order and u∈ℂ⁡[ℛn]u\in\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}] be an idempotent element. Define an mapping Su:ℂ⁡[ℛn]→ℂ⁡[ℛn],w↦w​uS_{u}:\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}]\rightarrow\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}],w\mapsto wu. The map SuS_{u} is ℂ\mathbb{C}-linear. The Peirce spectrum of ℂ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}] is the set of eigenvalues of operators SuS_{u} for all idempotent elements uu of ℂ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}]. The above technique is also helpful in computing the Peirce spectrum of ℂ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}] for nn odd.

Lemma 3.1.

Let ℂ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}] be the quandle ring of a dihedral quandle. Let ζ=ei​2​π/n\zeta=e^{i2\pi/n}. Then the set {fr;r∈ℤn}\{f_{r}\;;r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}\} where fr=∑x∈ℤnζr​x​exf_{r}=\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\zeta^{rx}e_{x} is a basis of ℂ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}] as ℂ\mathbb{C}-vector space.

Proof.

We prove that the set {fr;r∈ℤn}\{f_{r}\;;r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}\} is a linear independent set. Let ∑r∈ℤncr​fr=0\sum\limits_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}c_{r}f_{r}=0. Then ∑rcr​(∑x∈ℤnζr​x​ex)=0\sum\limits_{r}c_{r}\left(\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\zeta^{rx}e_{x}\right)=0, and so ∑x∈ℤn(∑r∈ℤncr​ζr​x)​ex=0\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\left(\sum\limits_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}c_{r}\zeta^{rx}\right)e_{x}=0. Since {ex;x∈ℤn}\{e_{x}\;;x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}\} is a basis of ℂ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}], so ∑r∈ℤncr​ζr​x=0\sum\limits_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}c_{r}\zeta^{rx}=0 for all x∈ℤnx\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}. Now we fix s∈ℤns\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}, multiply the previous equality by ζ−s​x\zeta^{-sx} and sum for all x∈ℤnx\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}. We get ∑x∈ℤn(∑r∈ℤncr​ζr​x)​ζ−s​x=∑r∈ℤncr​∑x∈ℤnζ(r−s)​x=0\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\left(\sum\limits_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}c_{r}\zeta^{rx}\right)\zeta^{-sx}=\sum\limits_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}c_{r}\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\zeta^{(r-s)x}=0. Now by Lemma 2.1, we get n​cs=0nc_{s}=0 and so cs=0c_{s}=0. Since ss is arbitrary, so cr=0c_{r}=0 for all r∈ℤnr\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}. The size of set {fr;r∈ℤn}\{f_{r}\;;r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}\} is nn, hence it spans ℂ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}]. ∎

Theorem 3.2.

The Peirce Spectrum of the complex quandle algebra of the dihedral quandle of odd order is {0,1,−1}\{0,1,-1\}.

Proof.

Let u=∑xax​exu=\sum\limits_{x}a_{x}e_{x} be an idempotent element of ℂ⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}]. Let ζ=ei​2​π/n\zeta=e^{i2\pi/n}. We define a^​(r)=∑x∈ℤnax​ζr​x\hat{a}(r)=\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{x}\zeta^{rx}. Compute the operator Su:ℂ⁡[ℛn]→ℂ⁡[ℛn],w↦w​uS_{u}:\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}]\rightarrow\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}],w\mapsto wu on the basis {fr;r∈ℤn}\{f_{r}\;;r\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}\}. We get

Su​(fr)=fr​u\displaystyle S_{u}(f_{r})=f_{r}u =(∑x∈ℤnζr​x​ex)⋅(∑y∈ℤnay​ey)\displaystyle=\left(\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\zeta^{rx}e_{x}\right)\cdot\left(\sum\limits_{y\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{y}e_{y}\right)
=∑x,y∈ℤnζr​x​ay​e2​y−x\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{x,y\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\zeta^{rx}a_{y}e_{2y-x}
=∑y∈ℤnay​ζ2​r​y​∑z∈ℤnζ−r​z​ez\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{y\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}a_{y}\zeta^{2ry}\sum\limits_{z\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\zeta^{-rz}e_{z}
=a^​(2​r)​f−r\displaystyle=\hat{a}(2r)f_{-r}

where the second last equality is obtained after substituting z=2​y−xz=2y-x. After applying SuS_{u} again we get Su2​(fr)=a^​(2​r)​Su​(f−r)=a^​(2​r)​a^​(−2​r)​frS_{u}^{2}(f_{r})=\hat{a}(2r)S_{u}(f_{-r})=\hat{a}(2r)\hat{a}(-2r)f_{r}. We denote P​(r)=a^​(r)​a^​(−r)P(r)=\hat{a}(r)\hat{a}(-r). Then the preceding equation becomes Su2​(fr)=P⁡(2​r)​frS^{2}_{u}(f_{r})=P(2r)f_{r}. Thus P⁡(2​r)P(2r) an eigenvalue of Su2S^{2}_{u}.

Now from Lemma 2.3, we have a^​(r)=a^​(−r)​a^​(2​r)\hat{a}(r)=\hat{a}(-r)\hat{a}(2r) for all r∈ℤnr\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}. Replace rr by −r-r, then we have a^​(−r)=a^​(r)​a^​(−2​r)\hat{a}(-r)=\hat{a}(r)\hat{a}(-2r). Multiplying these two equations gives P⁡(r)=P⁡(r)​P​(2​r)P(r)=P(r)P(2r) for all r∈ℤnr\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}. One possibility is P⁡(r)=0P(r)=0. If P⁡(r)≠0P(r)\neq 0, then P⁡(2​r)=1P(2r)=1. Repeating this, we get P⁡(2j​r)=1P(2^{j}r)=1 for j≥1j\geq 1. Since nn is odd, so for some jj, we have 2j​r≡r(modn)2^{j}r\equiv r\pmod{n} and so P⁡(r)=1P(r)=1. Thus, for r∈ℤnr\in\mathbb{Z}_{n} either P⁡(r)=0P(r)=0 or P⁡(r)=1P(r)=1.

Thus eigenvalues of Su2S_{u}^{2} belong to set {0,1}\{0,1\} and so the eigenvalues of SuS_{u} belongs to {0,1,−1}\{0,1,-1\}. The eigenvalue 00 is achieved by taking u=0u=0, we have Su​(w)=w​u=0S_{u}(w)=wu=0 for all w∈ℂ⁡[ℛn]w\in\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{R}_{n}]. For u=eju=e_{j}, and w=ejw=e_{j}, we get Su​(w)=w​u=ej​ej=ejS_{u}(w)=wu=e_{j}e_{j}=e_{j}. For u=eju=e_{j} and w=ex−e2​j−xw=e_{x}-e_{2j-x} for x≠jx\neq j. We get Su​(w)=w​u=(ex−e2​j−x)​ej=−(ex−e2​j−x)S_{u}(w)=wu=(e_{x}-e_{2j-x})e_{j}=-(e_{x}-e_{2j-x}).

∎

4. Nontrivial idempotents in ℤ⁡[Aff⁡(ℤp,f)]\mathbb{Z}[{\rm Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_{p},f)]

The counterexample to the conjecture 1.1 is given in [4, Theorem 5.1] in the integral quandle ring of affine latin quandle Aff⁡(ℤ37,f){\rm Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_{37},f), for f⁡(x)=18​xf(x)=18x.

Each quandle automorphism linearly extends to the quandle ring automorphism, thus we have Aut⁡(Q)⊆Aut⁡(ℤ⁡[Q]){\rm Aut}(Q)\subseteq{\rm Aut}(\mathbb{Z}[Q]). For an idempotent element u∈ℤ⁡[Q]u\in\mathbb{Z}[Q] and for f∈Aut⁡(ℤ⁡[Q])f\in{\rm Aut}(\mathbb{Z}[Q]), f⁡(u)f(u) is also an idempotent element since we have f​(u)2=f⁡(u2)=f⁡(u)f(u)^{2}=f(u^{2})=f(u). As an example, if we apply the automorphism ex↦ex+23e_{x}\mapsto e_{x+23} of ℤ⁡[Aff⁡(ℤ37,f)]\mathbb{Z}[{\rm Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_{37},f)] for f⁡(x)=18​xf(x)=18x, on the idempotent element of [4, 4,Theorem 5.1], we get the following.

Example 4.1.

Let Q=Aff⁡(ℤ37,f)Q={\rm Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_{37},f) be affine latin quandle on ℤ37\mathbb{Z}_{37} for f⁡(x)=18​xf(x)=18x then

u=\displaystyle u= e0+2​(e3+e4+e7+e30+e33+e34)\displaystyle e_{0}+2(e_{3}+e_{4}+e_{7}+e_{30}+e_{33}+e_{34})

is a nonzero idempotent in ℤ⁡[Q]\mathbb{Z}[Q].

For an affine latin quandle Q=Aff⁡(ℤp,f)Q={\rm Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_{p},f) of prime order, we prove that if ℤ⁡[Q]\mathbb{Z}[Q] has a nontrivial idempotent uu of augmentation 11, then with the help of such a nontrivial idempotent uu, we can construct infinitely many nontrivial idempotents in ℤ⁡[Q]\mathbb{Z}[Q].

Theorem 4.2.

Let the quandle ring ℤ⁡[Q]\mathbb{Z}[Q] for a connected quandle Q=Aff⁡(ℤp,f)Q={\rm Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_{p},f) have a nontrivial idempotent uu with augmentation 11. Then ℤ⁡[Q]\mathbb{Z}[Q] has infinitely many nontrivial idempotents.

Proof.

Let u=∑x∈ℤpax​ex∈ℤ⁡[Q]u=\sum\limits_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}}a_{x}e_{x}\in\mathbb{Z}[Q] be a nontrivial idempotent with augmentation 11. The coefficients of XzX^{z} modulo Xp−1X^{p}-1 in the above expression are exactly the coefficients of eze_{z} in u2u^{2}. Thus u2=uu^{2}=u in ℤ⁡[Q]\mathbb{Z}[Q] is equivalent to A⁡(Xt)​A​(Xs)=A⁡(X)A(X^{t})A(X^{s})=A(X) in RR.
